scenario: AITA for not ending my friendship with my best friend after he cheated on my sister? | Both my best friend and my sister know about my other account so this is a throwaway. I'm an 18 year old guy and I have a twin sister. I've been best friends with my best friend (we'll call him G) since kindergarten, so G and my sister have always been pretty close too. They've kind of had a "thing" going on our whole lives. For the longest time, they never officially dated for a bunch of different reasons I won't get into, but they were always really close and really into each other. A little over a year ago, when we were all 17, they finally started dating. Everything went really well for like 13 months, but then long story short, G cheated on my sister and I was the one who figured it out. He swore it wouldn't happen again and begged me not to tell my sister but I told her anyway. I was mad at him and he was mad at me so we didn't talk for a month and a half, which was honestly the weirdest month and a half of my whole life. G's practically like my brother, we've been inseparable since kindergarten, so not having him around was kinda....unbearable honestly lol After our streak of not talking to each other, G invited me on his family ski trip as a way to make amends (I've been on lots of his family's ski trips through the years). I accepted and ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it was way too weird without him in it. I can tell he's genuinely sorry about what happened. He literally cried cause he felt so bad and I've only seen him cry like once before in my whole life Anyway, G and my sister broke up as soon as she found out he cheated and they're still not on speaking terms, so my sister obviously isn't happy about the whole situation. She's making me feel like shit for still being friends with G, and she doesn't seem to understand how big of a deal it would be for us to lose our 13 year friendship over her. I know G made a huge mistake, I hate him for it and I'll never 100% get over it, but I'm not gonna let it ruin my best and longest friendship. I think about it like this: if your best friend cheated on their SO and then felt like shit, would you end your friendship with them? No. So why is this any different just because his SO happened to be my sister? G and I are going to the same college in the fall (a different college in a different state than the one my sister's going to), so none of this is gonna be something that we even think about when we're living in different places Am I the asshole?

We both got mad at each other and didn't talk for a month and a half, which was really weird and hard for me because G is like my brother. After that, G invited me on his family ski trip to make things right, and I went. I ended up forgiving him and letting him back into my life because it felt too weird without him around. He seems genuinely sorry, even cried about it, which I've only seen once before. Now, G and my sister broke up, and they're not speaking. My sister is upset with me for still being friends with G and doesn't understand why our 13-year friendship is more important than her feelings. I think about it like this: if my best friend cheated on their significant other and felt bad about it, would I end our friendship? Probably not. So why should it be different just because his SO is my sister? Plus, we're both going to the same college in the fall, so this might not even be an issue once we're in different places. So, am I the asshole for not ending my friendship with G after he cheated on my sister? First, I need to consider the dynamics of the relationships involved. G is not just any friend; he's been my best friend since kindergarten. That's a significant bond, built over years of shared experiences. My sister and G have also had a close relationship, almost like a love story that never fully blossomed until they started dating. The cheating incident is serious, and it's understandable that my sister is hurt and upset. However, I'm trying to balance my loyalty to G with my support for my sister. I think about the concept of forgiveness. G apologized, seemed genuinely remorseful, and took steps to make amends, like inviting me on the ski trip. Forgiveness doesn't mean forgetting, but it does mean moving past the hurt to some extent. I chose to forgive him because the absence of our friendship was too hard to bear, and I value our long-standing relationship. On the other hand, my sister feels betrayed, and it's natural for her to be upset with G. She might also feel that I'm prioritizing G's friendship over her feelings, which is a valid concern. It's a tough spot because I want to support my sister, but I also don't want to lose a friendship that's been so important to me. I also consider the future aspect. We're all moving to different colleges, so the immediate impact of this situation might diminish over time. Distance can help people move on and heal from such incidents. Another angle is the idea of personal boundaries and what I'm comfortable with. If G's actions make it difficult for me to maintain a healthy relationship with my sister, then maybe I need to reevaluate my friendship with G. However, if I feel that my friendship with G is worth preserving despite the conflict, then perhaps I'm not the asshole. I also think about the concept of loyalty. Am I being disloyal to my sister by continuing my friendship with G? Or am I being true to myself by valuing a friendship that's been significant in my life? It's a delicate balance between family loyalty and personal relationships. In the end, I have to decide what's best for me and my well-being. If maintaining the friendship with G brings me more happiness and doesn't negatively impact my relationship with my sister beyond what's already happened, then maybe it's not wrong to continue the friendship. However, if it's causing ongoing conflict or making my sister feel unsupported, then perhaps I need to reconsider. It's also important to communicate openly with both G and my sister about how I feel and what I need from the relationships. Clear communication can help bridge the gap and ensure that everyone's feelings are respected.
